data.title: Sequence of exchange of experts’ reports
sentences: (1) If a party intends to use the evidence of an expert at trial, the expert’s report must be served in the sequence described in subrule (2).

(a) the party who bears the primary onus of proof must serve on each of the other parties the report of that party’s expert
(b) the other party or parties must serve their expert’s rebuttal report, if any, and may include in the report issues not raised in the initial expert’s report

data.title: Objection to an expert’s report
data.text:
(1) A party who receives an expert’s report must notify the party serving the report of (a) any objection to the admissibility of the expert’s report that the party receiving the report intends to raise at trial, and (b) the reasons for the objection.
(2) No objection to the admissibility of an expert’s report is permitted at trial unless (a) reasonable notice of the objection was given to the other party, or (b) the Court permits the objection to be made.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.36 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
sentences: (1) A party who receives an expert’s report must notify the party serving the report of
(a) any objection to the admissibility of the expert’s report that the party receiving the report intends to raise at trial, and
(b) the reasons for the objection.
(2) No objection to the admissibility of an expert’s report is permitted at trial unless
(a) reasonable notice of the objection was given to the other party, or
(b) the Court permits the objection to be made. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.36 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
Rule 5.36 requires any party who wishes to object to the admissibility of an expert report to do so before trial. The purpose of this rule, along with rule 5.35, is to prevent surprise and unnecessary adjournments that may be required when the other party becomes aware of objections at trial. 1469753 Alberta Ltd. (c.o.b. Royal Services) v. Luxen, [2015] A.J. No. 476, 2015 ABQB 282 at para. 59 (Alta. Q.B.). Even where a party does not comply with rule 5.36, the court retains an overriding discretion to allow a party to object to admissibility of an expert’s report.
A party should not file a notice of objection of admissibility of an expert’s report.  Henderson (Estate) v. Arnett, [2011] A.J. No. 345, 2011 ABQB 198 at para. 14 (Alta. Q.B.).

data.title: Questioning experts before trial
sentences: (1) The parties may agree, or in exceptional circumstances the Court may direct, that an expert be questioned by any party adverse in interest to the party proposing to call the expert witness at trial.
(2) The questioning must be limited to the expert’s report.
(3) The Court may impose conditions about questioning with respect to all or any of the following:
(a) limiting the length of questioning
(b) specifying the place where the questioning is to take place
(c) directing payment of costs incurred

data.title: Continuing obligation on expert
data.text:
If, after an expert’s report has been provided by one party to another, the expert changes his or her opinion on a matter in the report, the change of opinion must be (a) disclosed by the expert in writing, and (b) immediately served on each of the other parties.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.38 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
sentences: If, after an expert’s report has been provided by one party to another, the expert changes his or her opinion on a matter in the report, the change of opinion must be
(a) disclosed by the expert in writing, and
(b) immediately served on each of the other parties. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.38 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text: Rule 5.38 provides that if an expert changes their reported opinion after service, they must disclose the change in writing and it must be served immediately to the other parties. The expert is not required to file any reports which outline a change of opinion with the courts. Henderson (Estate) v. Arnett, [2011] A.J. No. 345, 2011 ABQB 198 at para. 12 (Alta. Q.B.). However, vague notification of a change to an expert opinion on the eve of trial after years since the initial opinions may be a breach of rule 5.38 justifying exclusion of the changed opinion. Brenenstuhl (Guardian of) v. Caldwell, [2019] A.J. No. 354, 2019 ABQB 210 at para. 12 (Alta. Q.B.).

data.title: Use of expert’s report at trial without expert
data.text:
(1) A party serving an expert’s report may, at the same time, also serve notice of intention to have the report entered as evidence without calling the expert as a witness.
(2) If a party serves a notice of intention under subrule (1), no objection may months after service of the notice under subrule (1), any other party serves a statement on the party serving the notice of intention (a) setting out all or parts of the report that that other party objects to being entered as evidence under this rule, and giving reasons for the objection, or (b) serving on the party a request that the expert attend the trial for cross-examination.
(3) Agreeing to have the expert’s report entered as evidence without calling the expert as a witness, either explicitly or by allowing subrule (2) to operate without objection, is not an admission of the truth or correctness of the expert’s report.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.39 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.title: Expert’s attendance at trial
data.text:
(1) A party who agrees to have all of an expert’s report entered in evidence at trial, either explicitly or by allowing rule 5.39(2) [Use of expert’s report at trial without expert] to operate without objection, may, at the same time as responding to the notice of intention, serve a request that the expert be in attendance at trial for cross-examination.
(2) The expert whose entire report is to be entered at trial must not give oral evidence at trial unless (a) a request that the expert attend for cross-examination has been served, or (b) the Court permits.
(3) The party who requests an expert’s attendance for cross-examination must pay the costs of the expert’s attendance, determined under Schedule B [Court Fees and Witness and Other Allowances], unless the Court is satisfied that the cross-examination is of sufficient assistance to warrant a different order about who is to pay those costs.
(4) If the party proposing to enter the expert’s report receives a request that the expert attend for cross-examination, the party proposing to enter the report may question the expert at trial.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r.5.40 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

A party who serves a request that the expert be in attendance Notice must be given under this rule if a party agrees to the entry of an expert report at trial or permits rule 5.39(2) to operate without objection, but nonetheless wishes to cross-examine the expert.

hierarchy.heading: Division 3 – MEDICAL EXAMINATIONS BY HEALTH CARE PROFESSIONALS

rules.title: Medical examinations
rules.text:
(1) The parties may agree that the mental or physical condition of a person is at issue in an action and agree on a health care professional to conduct a medical examination.
(2) On application, the Court may in an action in which the mental or physical condition of a person is at issue do either or both of the following:
(a) order that a person submit to mental or physical medical examination;
(b) appoint a health care professional to conduct a medical examination.
(3) The Court may order a second or further medical examination by a health care professional.
(4) If the plaintiff has been the subject of a medical examination by a health care professional of the plaintiff’s choice who will or may be proffered as an expert, the Court may order that the plaintiff be the subject of a medical examination by one or more health care professionals of the defendant’s choice.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.41 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

(2) On application, the Court may in an action in which the mental or physical condition of a person is at issue do either or both of the following:
(a) order that a person submit to mental or physical medical examination
(b) appoint a health care professional to conduct a medical examination.
(3) The Court may order a second or further medical examination by a health care professional.

(4) If the plaintiff has been the subject of a medical examination by a health care professional of the plaintiff’s choice who will or may be proffered as an expert, the Court may order that the plaintiff be the subject of a medical examination by one or more health care professionals of the defendant’s choice. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.41 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
Rule 5.41 is broader than its predecessor under the Former Rules in two respects. First, the category of professionals who may conduct an examination (see definitions) is much broader. Second, an examination may be conducted of any person whose mental or physical condition may, in the opinion of the court, be at issue (rather than, in the past, only a plaintiff).
Where a person’s mental or physical condition is an issue in an action, rule 5.41 provides that the person may be required to submit to medical examinations. Where sought by defendants under rule 5.41(4), these are commonly referred to as “independent medical examinations” although they are performed by physicians engaged by the defendant.  Gordon v. Taylor Benc v. , [2014] A.J. No. 12, 2014 ABQB 11 at para. 21 (Alta. Q.B.), citing Parker, [2012] A.J. No. 885, 2012 ABCA 249 at para. 9 (Alta. C.A.). The purpose of these examinations is to enable the defendant to obtain evidence of a plaintiff’s mental or physical condition in order to present a full answer and defence. Kohlendorfer v. Northcott, [2013] A.J. No. 261, 2013 ABQB 145 at para. 32 (Alta. Q.B.), citing Lyons v. Khamsanevongsy, [1997] A.J. No. 762, 207 A.R. 385 at para. 22 (Alta. Q.B.).
Where one defendant has not made a claim over against another defendant, they are not considered to be the same party for the purpose of rule 5.41(4). Even when a single party seeks permission to call more than one expert at trial in a given area, that request will not be rejected where the applicant establishes relevance, necessity, absence of an exclusionary rule, and a properly qualified expert. Ewashko v. Hugo Smith v. , [2020] A.J. No. 659, 2020 ABCA 228 at para. 15 (Alta. C.A.), citing Obuck, [2018] A.J. No. 1484, 2018 ABQB 849 (Alta. Q.B.).
Timing – Defendants may wait to rely on rule 5.41 until after a plaintiff has disclosed its expert report(s) under rule 5.35.330 In other words, a defendant is not required to exercise their right to request a medical examination before the plaintiff submits any expert reports. Drapaka v. Patel, [2013] A.J. No. 423, 2013 ABQB 247 at paras. 41-42 (Alta. Q.B.).
“Mental or Physical Condition” – Rule 5.41 does not allow a court to order an individual to undergo DNA testing because a person’s DNA is not a “mental or physical condition” but a trait. Branson v. Branson, [2015] A.J. No. 458, 2015 ABQB 227 at para. 18 (Alta. Q.B.). Rather, the court will consider whether to grant an order requiring DNA testing

rules.title: Options during medical examination
sentences: (1) Unless otherwise ordered by the Court, a person who is to be the subject of a medical examination by a health care professional may elect to do one or more of the following:
(a) nominate a health care professional to be present during the medical examination
(b) videotape the medical examination
(c) make a word-for-word recording of the medical examination.
(2) The Court may
(a) define or limit the presence or role of the nominated health care professional
(b) direct that any part of the medical examination, including any standardized tests, not be recorded, and
(c) otherwise provide direction as to the conduct of the medical examination. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.42 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
Rule 5.42 allows the plaintiff undergoing a medical examination under rule 5.41 to have a nominee present, videotape the exam, and/or take detailed notes. This is a presumptive right and can only be altered by application to the courts. The underlying principle of this rule appears to be to protect the person being subjected to a court-ordered examination.
Court’s Discretion – The court may exercise its discretion by limiting the manner in which a defence medical examination under rule 5.41 is recorded or witnessed. The onus rests on the party seeking to dispense with the plaintiff’s options under rule 5.42(1) to satisfy the court that reasons justify depriving the plaintiff of his or her entitlement to have the medical examination recorded or attended by a nominee. rules.title: Payment of costs of medical examinations
rules.text:
(1) Unless the Court otherwise orders, the party who applies for the order for a medical examination must pay the cost of the medical examination.
(2) Unless the Court otherwise orders, the cost of (a) the attendance of a nominated health care professional at a medical examination, or (3) The party arranging for the videotaping or recording must provide a copy of the videotape or recording to the other party as soon as practicable after the medical examination is completed.
(4) The videotape or recording (a) may be shown or played at trial only with the Court’s permission, and (b) may only be used to verify events at the medical examination.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.43 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
Rule 5.43 outlines the permitted use of video and written recordings taken at medical examinations conducted under rule 5.41, and outlines who is to bear the costs of such procedures. Unlike usual cost rules which entitle a successful party to costs, the cost of video recordings and/or the attendance of a health care nominee at medical examinations is to be paid by the party requesting such procedures. Chisholm v. Lindsay, [2013] A.J. No. 1097, 2013 ABQB 589 at para. 47 (Alta. Q.B.); affd [2015] A.J. No. 572, 2015 ABCA 179 at para. 48 (Alta. C.A.). The requesting party is not responsible for up-front payment of the cost of attendance of a nominee or a videographer.
These costs can be sought by a plaintiff as a recoverable disbursement after trial. Khaleel v. Indar Dirk v. , [2024] A.J. No. 401, 2024 ABKB 203 at para. 68 (Alta. K.B.); see also Toews, [2020] A.J. No. 18, 2020 ABQB 16 (Alta. Q.B.).

Conduct of examination
rules.text:
(1) A health care professional conducting a medical examination may ask the person being examined questions relating to that person’s mental and physical condition and medical history, and the person being examined must answer the questions.
(2) If the person to be examined agrees in writing, or if the Court so orders, the examining health care professional may (3) The party causing the medical examination to be conducted (a) must, on request, deliver promptly to each of the other parties a copy of a detailed written report of the health care professional’s findings and conclusions, and (b) is, on request, entitled to receive promptly from the person examined a report of every medical examination previously or subsequently made of the physical or mental condition of the person resulting from the injuries sustained or the mental or physical condition that is in issue.
(4) If a party refuses to provide a report in the manner described in subrule (3), the Court may order the report to be provided, and if the health care professional refuses to make the report in writing, the Court may make any order it considers proper, one of the provisions of which may be the exclusion of the health care professional’s evidence if that person’s evidence is offered at trial.
(5) On application, the Court may make any order it considers necessary to limit or curtail a medical examination.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.44 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
Rule 5.44 sets out the types of questions that a medical professional is entitled to ask during an examination under rule 5.41, the samples or tests the medical professional may take or make during a medical examination if the examined party agrees in writing or the court so orders, the requirements relating to the disclosure of reports of the medical examination, and the court’s discretion to make any order it considers necessary to limit or curtail a medical examination. Nguyen v. Koehn, [2012] A.J. No. 1123, 2012 ABQB 655 at para. 15 (Alta. Q.B.).
“Samples” – Given the medical context of rule 5.44, the Court of Appeal has interpreted the word “samples” to be a broad word, which includes blood samples. Adacsi v. Amin, [2013] A.J. No. 988, 2013 ABCA 315 at para. 8 (Alta. C.A.).
“Examining Health Care Professional” – Rule 5.44(2) does not restrict who may obtain a sample or test from a person undergoing a medical examination. Adacsi v. Amin, [2013] A.J. No. 988, 2013 ABCA 315 at para. 9 (Alta. C.A.). This means that in addition to the medical professional conducting the examination, a court order to provide samples or undergo tests may be conducted by a qualified third party medical professional, such as a lab technician. Adacsi v. Amin, [2013] A.J. No. 988, 2013 ABCA 315 at para. 9 (Alta. C.A.).

rules.title: What this division applies to
sentences: This Division
(a) applies to every application filed in the Court unless a rule or an enactment otherwise provide or the Court otherwise orders or permits
(b) does not apply to originating applications unless the parties other- wise agree or the Court otherwise orders. 1 Throughout the Rules, “master” has been replaced by “applications judge”.

rules.title: Application to the Court to exercise its authority
rules.text:
When the Court has authority under these rules, a person may make an application to the Court that the Court exercise its authority.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.2 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*
sentences: When the Court has authority under these rules, a person may make an application to the Court that the Court exercise its authority. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.2 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

commentary.text:
Where the court has authority under the rules, this part applies to an application to have the court exercise that authority. It implicitly recognizes that litigation in Alberta, as in common law jurisdictions generally, is usually party driven.
Subdivision 1: APPLICATION PROCESS GENERALLY

rules.title: Applications generally
rules.text:
(1) Unless these rules or an enactment otherwise provides or the Court otherwise permits, an application may only be filed during an action or after judgment is entered.
(2) Unless the Court otherwise permits, an application the Court must (a) be in the appropriate form set out in Schedule A, Division 1 to the rules, (b) state briefly the grounds for filing the application, (c) identify the material or evidence intended to be relied on, (d) refer to any provision of an enactment or rule relied on, (e) specify any irregularity complained of or objection relied on, (f) state the remedy claimed or sought, and (g) state how the application is proposed to be heard or considered under these rules.
(3) Unless an enactment, the Court or these rules otherwise provide, the applicant must file and serve on all parties and every other person affected by the application,  Milavsky v. Milavsky Estate Reeves , [2016] A.J. No. 768, 2016 ABQB 410 at para. 106 (Alta. Q.B.); v. Grassi, [2019] A.J. No. 740, 2019 ABQB 416 at paras. 12-14 (Alta. Q.B.). days or more before the application is scheduled to be heard or considered, (a) notice of the application, and (b) any affidavit or other evidence in support of the application.

rules.title: Applications without notice
rules.text:
Despite any other rule to the contrary, notice of an application is not required to be served on a party if an enactment so provides or permits or the Court is satisfied that (a) no notice is necessary, or (b) serving notice of the application might cause undue prejudice to the applicant.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.4 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

commentary.text:
Applications with no notice are commonly referred to as ex parte applications. There are stringent professional and legal requirements where ex parte applications are brought, and they can only be brought where the law (whether common law or statute) permits. applications are exceptional, generally limited to situations Ex parte where “the delay associated with notice would result in harm or where there is a fear that the other party will act improperly or irrevocably if notice were given.” Ruby v. Canada (Solicitor General), [2002] S.C.J. No. 73, 2002 SCC 75 at para. 25 (S.C.C.), quoted in , [2017] A.J. No. 1082, 2017 ABCA 316 at para. Secure 2013 Group Inc. v. Tiger Calcium Services Inc. 41 (Alta. C.A.); see also , [2022] A.J. No. 374, 2022 South Side Manufacturing Ltd. v. SS Decking Ltd. ABCA 103 at para. 15 (Alta. C.A.) and , [2022] A.J. No. 8, 2022 ABQB 9 at para. Darby v. CitiFinancial 25 (Alta. Q.B.), for a useful summary with citations of the principles applicable to without-notice applications. It is only in exceptional circumstances that a court will make an order at the request of one party without giving the party or parties who are affected by the order the opportunity of opposing the order. Brousseau v. Foley, [2011] A.J. No. 1517, 2011 ABQB 813 at para. 8 (Alta. Q.B.). Rule 9.15(1)(a) expressly allows the court to set aside, vary or discharge an order made without notice.
